posts.title: Are You Automating Tasks, or Actually Building a Business?
posts.content:
The illusion of progress
We’re in a gold rush. Every week, a new vendor promises their latest AI feature will deliver "unprecedented productivity." And for anyone in a director or CXO seat, it’s a hard pitch to resist.

So licenses get purchased. A press release goes out. The organization is officially "AI-powered."
But let’s be honest with each other—buying seats isn’t a strategy. It’s an accounting entry.

What most organizations are actually doing right now is running a massive, uncoordinated productivity experiment. Throwing technology at the wall and hoping something sticks. It feels like progress. It rarely is. More often, it’s just a very expensive way of funding your own inefficiency.

Toys vs. tools—and why the difference matters
If you want to move from experimenting to actually building something institutional, you need to get clear on one distinction: what’s a toy in your organization, and what’s a tool?

The toy is what I call the Shadow AI problem. It’s the employee pasting a sensitive product roadmap into a public chatbot because it’s faster than using the approved system. They’re not being more productive—they're quietly creating a security liability that nobody has quantified yet. This is the "wild west" phase of AI adoption, and most organizations are still deep in it.

The tool is something engineered. It’s connected to your proprietary data, it behaves predictably where it needs to, and it’s built to be right at scale—not just fast. There’s a world of difference between the two, and right now, most boardrooms are funding toys while expecting tools.

The data debt nobody wants to talk about
Before we get to algorithms and models, we need to talk about something less exciting but far more important: data debt.

Here’s my reality as an AI/ML engineer—I spend roughly 80% of my time on data preparation. The actual model? That’s the last 20%. If your leadership team is waiting for the AI to magically fix your data architecture, I can tell you now how that project ends.

The hard truth is that you cannot build a modern AI system on a foundation of siloed, inconsistent, or legacy data. It simply doesn’t work.
So the question directors need to stop asking is "Why isn’t the AI performing?" The question they need to start asking is "What does our data pipeline actually look like?" The unglamorous, foundational work of data governance isn’t optional—it's the prerequisite for everything else.

Governance isn’t IT’s problem—it's yours.
AI is the first technology where the risk profile isn’t just technical. It’s ethical and legal too.

How is your organization handling personally identifiable information inside AI workflows? What happens when a model confidently generates a customer commitment that turns out to be completely wrong? These aren’t hypothetical edge cases anymore.

And here’s the part that often gets missed: Governance cannot be delegated entirely to the IT department. It belongs in the boardroom.

Defining your organization's risk tolerance for AI is a business decision—not an engineering one. Are you willing to trade accuracy for speed? That’s a trade-off leadership needs to own.

The "build vs. buy" trap
One of the most common mistakes I see—especially in organizations trying to move fast—is attempting to mirror what the big tech companies are doing without having remotely similar infrastructure.

Most companies don’t need to build a foundational AI model from scratch. What they actually need is the connective tissue—the systems that link existing models to their specific business processes, data, and workflows.

And while we’re at it, stop measuring AI success by adoption rates or number of prompts run. Those metrics tell you very little. Start measuring by cost-per-unit-of-work saved or speed-to-market improvement. If you can’t connect your AI investment to a real business outcome, you don’t have a tool yet—you have a very expensive experiment.

Three questions for your next Monday meeting
If you want to start moving from toys to tools, try these on your direct reports this week:
"How are we quantifying the ROI of our current AI initiatives—and are we measuring them against our actual KPIs?"
"What security and compliance guardrails do we have in place, and do they cover everything our teams are using today?"
"Is our data genuinely ready for AI, or are we spending most of our time cleaning up after our own tools?"

The answers will tell you exactly where you stand.
The bottom line
The organizations that define their industries over the next decade won’t be the ones that bought the most licenses.

They’ll be the ones that treated AI as a genuine strategic shift—and did the hard, unglamorous groundwork to back it up.
You don’t need more AI right now. You need more clarity.

You don’t need more experiments. You need more infrastructure.
That’s your reality check for this week.

posts.title: Boardroom AI: Monday Reality Check
posts.content:
There’s a directive echoing through boardrooms right now, and you’ve almost certainly heard it: "We need to integrate AI."

But here’s what usually happens next—a lot of nodding, a few expensive pilots, and mounting frustration with very little to show for it.

We’re drowning in AI noise. And for the directors, department heads, and CXOs actually held accountable for results, the gap between the hype and the reality has never felt wider.
I’ve spent my career as an AI/ML engineer building these systems from scratch. Which means I see the stuff that never makes it onto the executive slide deck—the data silos, the scalability assumptions that fall apart under real conditions, and the chasm between a slick demo and something that actually moves the needle on ROI.

When I talk to leaders, the frustration isn’t usually with the technology. It’s that nobody is giving them a straight answer about what it actually takes to make it work.

So here’s why I’m starting this series.

Every Monday, I’ll be cutting through the noise with one clear, grounded insight—no technical rabbit holes, no miracle-cure promises. Just a high-signal briefing for the people responsible for the bottom line and the long game.

Each week, I’ll be focused on three things that actually matter at the executive level:
Risk—the hidden liabilities sitting inside your current AI roadmap
Readiness—whether your organization is actually set up for AI or needs a foundation reset first
ROI—shifting the conversation from "how do we use AI?" to "what specific problem are we solving?"

My commitment to you is simple. By the time your first Monday meeting kicks off, you’ll have one perspective-shifting insight you can actually use—whether that’s challenging a flawed assumption or giving your team a sharper direction.
This series is for leaders who are done chasing the hype cycle and want to build something that lasts.

Now I want to hear from you.
What’s the biggest AI frustration coming up in your boardroom right now? Is it the cost? The uncertainty? Data quality? The team’s ability to deliver?

Drop it in the comments or send me a message. Let’s make this a two-way conversation—because the reality check your organization needs probably starts with saying the quiet part out loud.

posts.title: How Uber Matches Riders and Drivers
posts.content:
Open the Uber app, tap “Request Ride,” and within seconds you have a driver’s name, a photo, a number plate, and an ETA. It feels instant. Almost thoughtless.

It is absolutely not.

What just happened in those few seconds involved demand forecasting, geospatial matching, real-time routing, dynamic pricing, and a continuous feedback loop—all running simultaneously, across a city full of people making completely unpredictable decisions. I think about this every time I book a ride. The app is almost insultingly simple to use. The system underneath it is anything but.

Let’s get into it.

The problem Uber is actually solving

Here’s the thing people don’t really think about: Uber isn’t matching you to a car. It’s trying to balance a live marketplace of two groups of people who want fundamentally different things.

Riders want to be picked up quickly, at a price that feels reasonable. Drivers want enough steady demand that the time spent on the road is actually worth it. These two things don’t naturally align. Demand spikes on Friday evenings. Drivers tend to cluster in neighborhoods they know. A concert ends and ten thousand people open the app at the same moment. Someone needs a ride from a quiet corner of the city at 2am.

Every technical decision Uber makes flows from one goal: take that messy, unpredictable real-world situation and bring it into balance, continuously, in real time. That’s the whole game.

Seeing the city as a grid

Before Uber can balance anything, it needs to understand what’s actually happening across a city at any given moment. And you can’t manage a city if you’re thinking about it as one big blob.

So the system breaks every city into small geographic zones—a grid of cells, each covering a few city blocks. At any moment, Uber knows how many requests are coming out of each cell, how many available drivers are in or near each cell, and critically, how both of those numbers are moving. Is demand in this area climbing? Has supply in the next zone just dropped because three drivers ended their shifts?

This sounds almost mundane when you describe it. But it’s the foundation everything else sits on. It turns an incomprehensibly complex city into something the system can actually reason about and act on in real time.

The matching engine: making a hard decision look easy

When you request a ride, something genuinely difficult happens very quickly. The system can’t just find the nearest driver and call it done—nearest on a map and nearest in terms of actual arrival time are completely different things. A driver two blocks away stuck at a bottleneck might be a far worse match than a driver six blocks away on a clear road heading in your direction already.

So the matching engine is weighing several things at once. Proximity, yes. But also estimated arrival time given live traffic. Whether the driver is fully free or just finishing another ride. Which direction they’re already moving. A driver already heading toward you is a better match than one who has to double back—even if the map distance looks worse.

And here’s the part that I find genuinely impressive: Uber isn’t solving one match at a time. It’s looking at batches of requests across a zone and trying to find the best set of matches simultaneously. Giving one great driver to one rider might leave three other riders badly served. The system tries to optimize across the whole picture, not just the individual pairing in front of it.

All of this happens in milliseconds. Because every second of delay is a second added to your wait.

Surge pricing: the part everyone hates, and why it actually works

I’ll be honest—surge pricing is genuinely annoying to experience. Opening the app and seeing a 2.4x multiplier on a rainy evening feels like being punished for needing a ride at the wrong time.

But from a systems perspective, it’s one of the more elegant solutions I’ve come across.

When demand in a zone outstrips supply, prices go up. This does two things simultaneously. Some riders see the higher price and decide to wait fifteen minutes or find another option—demand softens. Meanwhile, drivers see their earnings-per-hour climbing and either stay on the road longer or move toward that zone—supply increases. The market rebalances itself, automatically, without anyone making a manual decision.

The reverse works too. Quiet periods trigger driver incentives—bonuses for completing a certain number of rides, guaranteed minimums—to ease supply back down to a level that makes sense.

The reason surge pricing makes people so angry is that it’s most visible in the moments when you most need a ride. But it’s also exactly why a ride is available at all in those moments. Without it, the system tips out of balance, and nobody can get anything.

ETA: where the system earns or loses your trust

The estimated arrival time sitting on your screen when you book a ride is doing more work than it looks like.

It’s not a rough guess. It’s a prediction built from live traffic data, historical patterns for that specific route at that specific time of day, the driver’s current position, and the complexity of the pickup itself. Uber puts real effort into getting this right because the consequences of getting it wrong are subtle but significant.

If the app tells you four minutes and the driver shows up in nine, you’ve had a bad experience before you’ve even sat down. Do that consistently and people stop trusting the number. They start hovering anxiously instead of getting on with their day. The ETA is one of those things that only gets noticed when it’s wrong.

Routing doesn’t stop at the moment you book, either. If traffic shifts while the driver is on their way to you, the system already knows and has already recalculated. Live adjustment, not just live prediction.

This matters for drivers just as much as riders. An efficient route means less dead time, more rides completed, and better earnings. The routing engine is quietly serving both sides of the marketplace at once.

The feedback loop: how the system gets smarter

Every single ride generates a signal. Whether you cancelled before the driver arrived. Whether the driver cancelled on you. How close the actual pickup time was to the predicted one. How you rated the experience. Whether you opened the app again the following week.

All of that flows back in. Cancellation patterns teach the matching engine which pairings tend to fail—maybe certain kinds of pickups at certain hours have a high drop-off rate, so those should be weighted differently next time. ETA data refines the routing models. Ratings surface patterns that aggregate data alone might miss.

The system isn’t fixed. It’s recalibrating constantly, using what actually happened to sharpen what it predicts next time. Each ride is a service and a data point simultaneously.

This feedback loop is honestly what separates a decent marketplace from a formidable one. Getting a single match right is a tractable engineering problem. Building something that gets progressively better across millions of rides, in hundreds of cities, through wildly varying demand conditions—that's genuinely hard. And it’s where the real competitive advantage lives.

Where it breaks, because it does break

New cities are hard. A new market with a thin driver base and no historical ride data gives the system almost nothing to work with. Predictions are rougher, matching is less efficient, and the experience suffers until enough rides have happened to calibrate things properly.

Surge pricing has a fairness problem that doesn’t have a clean solution. The areas where supply is chronically low tend to be lower-income neighborhoods where residents have fewer alternatives. The mechanism optimizes for market balance, not for equitable access. Uber knows this. It’s not solved.

And genuine demand shocks—an entire stadium emptying at once, a weather event, a city-wide disruption—push the system into territory it wasn’t really designed for. ETAs become unreliable. Surge multipliers spike in ways that feel punitive. The system is technically doing exactly what it was built to do, and the experience is still awful. That tension doesn’t fully go away.

What I keep coming back to

The ride is the product. The system is the advantage.

Any well-funded team can build an app that connects riders to drivers. What took years to get right—and what’s genuinely difficult to replicate—is the optimization layer underneath. The demand forecasting, the matching logic, the pricing mechanism, the routing models, and the feedback loops that make all of it smarter over time.

That’s not the app. That’s the moat.

At its core, the whole system is solving one problem, over and over, millions of times a day: given imperfect information about where supply and demand are right now, make the best possible decision in the next few milliseconds.

Do that well enough, at a sufficient scale, and you’re not just booking rides.

You’re controlling the market.

This breakdown is based on publicly available information, observed product behavior, and industry-standard system design patterns. It doesn’t represent internal or proprietary Uber architecture.

posts.title: Netflix’s Recommendation Engine – How It Decides What You Watch Next
posts.content:
You know that feeling. You open Netflix, you’re genuinely in the mood to watch something, and twenty minutes later you’re still scrolling. Nothing looks quite right. You hover over a few things, read half a description, and somehow end up rewatching something you’ve already seen.

That experience—frustrating as it is—is the result of one of the most sophisticated recommendation systems ever built. And it’s worth understanding, because it’s not just picking shows you might like. It’s making decisions about your attention, your time, and, in a very real sense, whether you stay subscribed.

Let’s open it up.

Why recommendations are the whole business
Netflix has a simple core problem: out of thousands of titles, what should appear in front of you right now?
It sounds like a small UX question. It isn’t. Around 80% of what people watch on Netflix comes directly from a recommendation. Not searching, not browsing—a recommendation. Get it wrong consistently and people stop finding things they want to watch. They churn. They cancel. The stakes are enormous.

The problem actually breaks into three distinct challenges. First, candidate generation—taking a library of millions of titles and narrowing it down to a few hundred realistic options for you. Second, ranking—ordering those options by how likely you are to actually watch them and enjoy them. Third, the tension between familiarity and discovery—showing you things you’ll definitely like while still nudging you toward things you didn’t know you’d love.

Netflix frames this as a long-term value problem. The goal isn’t to get you to click something tonight. It’s to keep you satisfied enough that you’re still here next month.

What the engine actually knows about you
Every time you interact with Netflix, you’re generating data. Some of it is obvious—ratings, thumbs up, thumbs down, and things you add to your list. But most of it is implicit, and that’s where things get interesting.
How long you watched before stopping. Whether you finished. Whether you came back to something, you paused. What time of day do you watch? What device are you on? How long your sessions typically run. All of it feeds into the system.

From this, Netflix builds two kinds of profiles. A user embedding—essentially a numerical fingerprint of who you are as a viewer, your genre preferences, your binge patterns, and how often you finish things. And an item embedding—a fingerprint for each show or film, capturing genre, tone, cast, how fresh it is, and how similar it is to other things.

These embeddings are learned, not programmed. The system figures out the patterns itself from billions of interactions across hundreds of millions of users.

The two-stage pipeline: speed first, depth second
Here’s where the engineering gets clever. Netflix can’t run a deep, complex model across its entire library every time you open the app. That would be impossibly slow. So the system works in two stages.

Stage one is retrieval. This is the fast pass—taking thousands of titles down to a few hundred candidates in under 100 milliseconds. Simple, efficient models do this work. Item-based similarity ("people who watched this also watched that"). Collaborative filtering ("users who look like you liked this"). Embedding-based nearest neighbor search. Netflix runs several of these in parallel, each feeding a different ""lane"—Trending Now, Because You Watched, New Releases, and so on.

Stage two is ranking. Now the candidates go through something much more powerful—a deep neural network that scores each one against multiple signals simultaneously.

Will you click it? Will you actually watch it? Will you finish it? Each of these gets its own probability estimate, and they get combined into a single score that determines the order you see things in.

Training this ranking model happens on billions of real interactions. Crucially, it’s optimizing for actual watch time, not just clicks. A clickable thumbnail that leads to a disappointing show is a bad outcome by design.

The application layer—where the real engineering lives
The model is only part of the story. What I find most interesting is everything built around it.

When you look at your Netflix homepage, you’re seeing the output of a system that’s doing far more than running a ranking algorithm. Product rules determine how many items appear in each row, how much space new releases get, and how to balance movies against shows against Netflix originals. Different rows map to different retrieval channels. The ranking is optimized per slot, then aggregated into a homepage that has to feel coherent and useful rather than just algorithmically correct.

Then there’s the experimentation layer. Netflix uses a bandit-style approach to A/B testing—essentially, for a slice of users, recommendations are deliberately tweaked, and the system watches what happens to watch time, retention, and churn. This is how Netflix decides which unknown indie film deserves a push versus which proven hit should be surfaced again. It’s continuous, real-time learning about what the platform should be doing.

Cold start is another genuinely hard problem. What do you show a brand new user with no history? What do you do with a new show that nobody’s watched yet? Netflix handles this through global popularity signals and content-based matching—using what a show is to find audiences who’d likely respond to it, before there’s any behavioral data to rely on.

And then there’s latency. Recommendations have to load in under 200 milliseconds for hundreds of millions of users simultaneously. Embeddings are pre-computed and cached. Approximate nearest-neighbor search tools like FAISS make vector lookups fast enough to be practical at scale. The model accuracy you see is inseparable from the infrastructure built to serve it.

Where it breaks
No honest teardown skips this part.
The echo chamber problem is real. If the system over-optimizes for engagement, it can trap you in a narrow slice of what you’ve already shown interest in. You liked one thriller, so now your homepage is 60% thrillers, and you never discover that you’d actually love a particular documentary series.

Short-term and long-term satisfaction often pull in different directions. A provocative thumbnail gets clicks. That doesn’t mean the show was good or that the user will feel satisfied tomorrow. Netflix knows this, but measuring long-term satisfaction is genuinely hard, so the system’s incentives still skew toward what’s measurable right now.

Historical bias is baked into the data. If certain kinds of content were historically surfaced more to certain audiences, that pattern gets learned and reinforced. Netflix counters this with diversity metrics and fairness constraints in the objective functions—but it’s an ongoing battle, not a solved problem.

Myths worth clearing up
"The system knows what I like."

It doesn’t know anything, in any meaningful sense. It has identified statistical patterns—users who behaved similarly to you responded well to X, so there’s a good chance you will too. If you accidentally binge one niche genre, it might overcorrect for months.

"Recommendations are just about what’s popular."

Popularity is one signal, but watch time and completion rate matter more. A massively popular show can still rank low for you if people tend to quit it halfway through or if it’s already been pushed hard to your demographic.

"A bad recommendation means the system is broken."

The system is optimized for aggregate behavior across hundreds of millions of people. It expects to be wrong sometimes—that's built in. Some of those wrong suggestions are intentional exploration, testing whether you might like something outside your usual patterns.

"Long-term satisfaction is what Netflix actually optimizes for."

Engineers care about it. But the metrics that actually drive decisions are watch time, retention, and churn. Satisfaction is real but indirect and hard to measure cleanly—so in practice the system often behaves more like a short-term engagement engine, with longer-term well-being as a secondary consideration.

Next week: AI search engines

We’re going deep on how AI-powered search actually works—retrieval-augmented generation, how results get ranked and filtered, and the decisions that determine what you see when you type a question into a search bar.

If there’s a system you want torn down, drop it in the comments. See you next week.

posts.title: Under the Hood: AI Systems - A Weekly Look at How This AI Stuff Actually Works
posts.content:
I’ll be honest with you—I got tired of not knowing.
Not tired of AI. Tired of the gap between watching something impressive and actually understanding what just happened. You see a demo, you’re genuinely amazed, and then someone asks, "But how does it work?" and the best answer most of us have is a vague hand-wave toward "neural networks" or "it’s trained on a lot of data."

That gap bothered me enough to do something about it. So I’m starting this series.
Every week, we take one AI system or application and open it up completely. Not the marketing version. The real version—architecture, training, the messy trade-offs, and the reasons things break. The stuff that usually lives in whitepapers nobody reads or research threads that assume you already have a PhD.

The thing I actually care most about
Here’s what I haven’t seen done well anywhere and what I want this series to be known for.

Most AI explainers stop at the model. They walk you through how attention works, maybe explain backpropagation, and then wrap up. And that’s genuinely useful—but it’s half the picture at best.

What nobody talks about enough is how AI applications are actually built. Not the model sitting in a research lab. The thing someone opens on their laptop and uses every day.
How does ChatGPT decide when to search the web and when to answer from memory? What’s actually happening when GitHub Copilot streams a suggestion into your editor in under a second? How does a customer support bot maintain context across a conversation, stay on topic, and still know when it’s out of its depth?
Those questions live in the layer around the model—the orchestration, the memory systems, the retrieval pipelines, the prompt architecture, and the decisions about latency and cost and failure modes. That’s where most of the interesting engineering actually happens. And that’s where we’re going to spend a lot of our time.

What to expect each week
Every post follows a similar shape. We start with the big picture—why this system matters and what problem it’s solving. Then we get into the mechanics, with real diagrams and the equations that actually matter (not just the ones that look impressive). We look at how it’s trained, how it’s optimized, and where it tends to break.
And then—the part I’m most excited about—we look at how it becomes a real application. What does the full stack look like? What decisions did the builders have to make, and what did those decisions cost them? Where are the hard problems hiding that the demos never show you?
I’ll also include something small you can run yourself most weeks. Because reading about how diffusion models work is one thing. Watching one denoise an image step by step in a notebook you’re actually running is something else entirely.

Who I’m writing this for
Honestly? Anyone who’s curious and done with being talked down to.

If you’re an engineer who uses AI tools every day but wants to understand them at a deeper level—this is for you. If you work in product or business and you’re tired of nodding along in technical conversations you only half follow—this is for you. If you’re just someone who finds this stuff fascinating and wants to actually get it—absolutely for you.
We’ll also knock down some myths along the way, because there are a lot of them. AI doesn’t understand language in any meaningful sense—it's predicting the next most likely token, over and over, at an extraordinary scale. Bigger models aren’t automatically better—thoughtful architecture regularly beats brute-force size. And "just call the API" is rarely as simple as it sounds when you’re building something real.

One small taste before we begin
In a transformer, self-attention lets every word in a sentence look at every other word at the same time. Take: "The bank by the riverbank collapsed."
A model without self-attention might easily confuse the two meanings of "bank." With it, the presence of "river" quietly shifts the interpretation of the first "bank" toward water, not finance. The ambiguity dissolves—naturally, in parallel, across the whole sentence at once.

That moment where something clicks—that's what I’m chasing every week.
Come along.
New posts drop weekly, here on the blog and in a shorter form on LinkedIn. If there’s a system you’ve always wanted to understand properly—how Perplexity actually retrieves and ranks information, what’s really going on inside an AI coding agent, how voice models convert sound into meaning—drop it in the comments. I mean it when I say I’ll read them.

The first deep dive is coming soon.

Let’s actually understand this thing.

posts.title: Beginner’s AI Blueprint - A Weekly Roadmap to Actually Understanding AI (Starting From Zero)
posts.content:
Hey, welcome—really glad you’re here.

If you’ve ever seen terms like "neural networks" or "deep learning" and quietly closed the tab, this series was made for you.

No judgment. AI can feel like it belongs to a special club of math geniuses and hardcore coders—and most learning resources do absolutely nothing to help that impression.

This one’s different. I’m starting from zero, and we’re going at a pace that actually makes sense.
So why am I doing this?
AI is quietly reshaping pretty much everything around us—the shows Netflix suggests, the route Google Maps picks, and even how doctors detect disease earlier. It’s fascinating stuff. But whenever I looked for beginner resources, they’d either drown me in jargon or assume I already knew Python and calculus.

So I decided to just build the series I wish had existed when I started.

Here’s the rough plan:

Weeks 1–4—We get the foundations right. What AI actually is, the key ideas behind it, and some simple tools you can play with. Zero code required.

Weeks 5–12—We get our hands dirty. A gentle intro to Python, and your very first ML models (they’re more approachable than they sound, I promise).

Week 13 onwards—The exciting stuff. Neural networks, real projects, and eventually deploying something you actually built.

One post a week. Short enough to read with your morning coffee, practical enough that you’ll actually learn something.

Every week you’ll get:
Explanations that use real, everyday examples (seriously—if I can’t explain it simply, I’ll try again until I can). Step-by-step guides, free tools, and small challenges to test what you’ve learned. And absolutely no assumed knowledge—just bring your curiosity.

That’s it. No prerequisites, no gatekeeping.
I’d love to know—what's your biggest question about AI right now? Drop it in the comments. There are no silly questions here, and your question might just shape a future post.

I’ll see you every week.

Let’s build something together.
